(3) Insurance lead generation platforms and marketing automation tools (InsuranceLeads.com, SmartFinancial, EverQuote, NetQuote selling exclusive and shared leads to agents at $15-$150 per auto/home lead and $50-$500 per life insurance lead, with active agents purchasing 50-500 leads/month = $750-$75,000/month spend, Contactability and AgencyBloc marketing automation at $200-$1,000/month for drip campaigns and client retention) where one high-volume agency spending $10K-$75K/month on leads = 50×-375× database cost just in first month; (4) Continuing education (CE) providers and professional training companies (state-mandated CE requirements for license renewal: 24 hours every 2 years typical across most states, with CE courses priced at $20-$200 per course and designation programs like CLU, ChFC, CPCU at $2,000-$8,000 for multi-course certification, WebCE, Kaplan Financial Education, The Institutes offering Risk Management Society CPCU designation) selling to 1.5M licensed agents who must complete CE every 2 years generating $30M-$300M annual CE market; (5) Carrier appointment services and agency consulting firms (helping new agents secure appointments with top carriers like State Farm, Allstate, Nationwide, Travelers, Progressive requiring minimum production standards and E&O coverage, with consulting fees of $5,000-$50,000 for agency startup consulting, technology implementation, M&A advisory for agency acquisitions at 5-10% of deal value = $50,000-$500,000 for $1M-$5M agency purchases, and perpetual agency growth consultants at $2,000-$10,000/month retainers). Total addressable market: Insurance Agent Lists reports 1.5M+ licensed insurance agents nationwide (combining Life & Health licenses and Property & Casualty licenses, with many agents holding both), National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC) data shows approximately 900,000 active P&C agents and 600,000 life & health agents (overlap creates ~1.5M unique individuals), and U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reports 531,000 insurance sales agent jobs as of 2026 (excludes independent contractors and part-time agents, significantly undercounting true TAM). Estimated 800,000-1,000,000 decision-maker contacts targeting active full-time agents and agency principals (excludes inactive licenses and part-time agents unlikely to purchase software/services), concentrated in major insurance markets (California 150K+ agents, Texas 125K+, Florida 110K+, New York 85K+, Pennsylvania, Illinois, Ohio, Georgia per state DOI licensing data). Public data is 100% accessible via state insurance department databases: all 50 states plus DC maintain searchable online licensing databases for insurance producers (agents and brokers) as mandated by state insurance codes requiring public transparency and consumer protection — California Department of Insurance License Search (insurance.ca.gov/01-consumers/120-company/07-license), Texas Department of Insurance Agent Lookup (tdi.texas.gov/agent), Florida Office of Insurance Regulation Agent & Agency Search, New York DFS Insurance Producer Search, NIPR (National Insurance Producer Registry) aggregating multi-state license data — with public fields including agent legal name, license number, license type/lines of authority (Property, Casualty, Life, Health, Variable Annuities, Personal Lines, Commercial Lines), license status (Active, Inactive, Suspended, Revoked), issue date, expiration date, resident state, agency name (if affiliated), agency address, and disciplinary actions. Engineering lift is moderate: scrape or download bulk licensing data from 50 state insurance department databases (many states offer CSV exports or open data portals, e.g., California DOI publishes weekly license updates), normalize license types and lines of authority across state-specific terminology (California 'Fire & Casualty' = Texas 'Property and Casualty', 'Disability' = 'Accident & Health' in some states), deduplicate multi-state licenses for agents operating across state lines (many agents hold resident license in home state plus non-resident licenses in 5-20 additional states for cross-border sales), filter for active full-time agents (exclude inactive, suspended, revoked licenses, and individuals with only CE provider or adjuster licenses), enrich with email/phone via business directory lookups (ZoomInfo, Apollo for agency principals, LinkedIn for individual agents, agency website scraping for contact forms), classify by agent type (captive agent for single carrier like State Farm/Allstate vs. independent agent representing multiple carriers, agency owner vs. producer), and segment by specialization (personal lines auto/home, commercial P&C, life insurance, health/benefits, financial services). No affordable flat-file competitor exists below $200 on Gumroad — all existing vendors (7+ identified) use enterprise 'contact for quote' pricing with typical B2B patterns of $0.15-$0.40 per contact = $9,000-$24,000 for 60,000-record targeted list (e.g., all P&C agents in California with active licenses), and subscription-based models requiring annual renewals for ongoing data updates, making a $149-$199 one-time CSV deliver unprecedented value (99% savings vs. enterprise pricing, instant access vs. 3-5 day quote-to-delivery timelines, no minimum order quantities vs. typical 5,000-record minimums). Score is 8 due to: (a) exceptionally strong commercial ecosystem with 7+ active vendors and massive TAM (1.5M licensed agents, $1.3 trillion in U.S. insurance premiums generating $30B-$50B in agent commissions annually per Insurance Information Institute), (b) ultra-high buyer LTV across all five segments (agency management software $15K-$3M lifetime, E&O insurance $1,500-$500K/year, lead generation $9K-$900K/year, CE providers $30M-$300M total market, consulting $5K-$500K per engagement) where 1-2 customer acquisitions justify 75×-15,000× database investment, (c) large and highly engaged TAM (800K-1M active full-time agents, all legally required to maintain licenses creating captive audience for CE and E&O), (d) 100% public data via state insurance department licensing databases (statutory transparency requirements, free online lookup and bulk downloads in many states), (e) clear buyer pain points and validated demand (agents actively seek leads, software to manage book of business, CE credits for license renewal, carrier appointments for commission income), and (f) significant pricing wedge vs. enterprise vendors charging $9K-$24K for targeted lists. Score not higher than 8 due to: (a) moderate engineering complexity requiring normalization across 50+ state-specific licensing schemas and terminology (though NIPR provides some standardization, individual state databases still require custom scraping), (b) high duplication rate for multi-state licenses requiring careful deduplication logic to avoid counting same agent 10-15 times (some agents hold non-resident licenses in 20+ states), (c) need for email/phone enrichment since most state databases contain only agency mailing addresses without direct agent email/mobile (though agency principals and independent agents have findable contact info via business directories, captive agents employed by State Farm/Allstate may lack public emails), and (d) mix of full-time career agents (high purchase intent for software/leads) vs. part-time agents and inactive licenses (low intent) requiring filtering to optimize list quality vs. raw size.

data_wanted: State insurance department licensing databases (all 50 states plus DC maintain public online producer/agent licensing systems as mandated by state insurance codes requiring transparency and consumer protection): California Department of Insurance License Search (insurance.ca.gov/01-consumers/120-company/07-license) covering 150K+ licensed agents with searchable interface by name, license number, or agency, providing agent legal name, license number, license type (Life-Only, Accident & Health, Fire & Casualty Broker-Agent, Personal Lines, Property Broker, Surplus Lines), license status (Active, Cancelled, Expired, Surrendered, Suspended, Revoked), issue date, expiration date, agency affiliation, mailing address, and disciplinary actions; Texas Department of Insurance Agent Lookup (tdi.texas.gov/agent) for 125K+ Texas resident agents; Florida Office of Insurance Regulation Agent & Agency Information Search for 110K+ Florida producers; New York Department of Financial Services Insurance Producer Search for 85K+ NY agents; Illinois, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Georgia, North Carolina, Michigan, Virginia, Arizona, Washington DOI licensing portals — most states offer free web-based lookup with no authentication required, and many provide bulk CSV exports or open data portals (e.g., California DOI publishes weekly license update files, Florida OIR offers data downloads). National Insurance Producer Registry (NIPR) at nipr.com provides centralized multi-state license lookup showing all non-resident licenses held by agents operating across state lines, useful for deduplication (count each agent once in resident state, not 10-15 times across all non-resident states). Target data fields per record: Agent legal name (first, middle, last), personal license number, resident state license number, non-resident state licenses (if applicable), license type/lines of authority (normalize across state-specific terminology: Property, Casualty, Property & Casualty, Personal Lines, Commercial Lines, Life, Accident & Health, Health, Variable Contracts/Annuities, Surplus Lines, Travel, Credit), license status (Active, Inactive, Expired, Suspended, Revoked, Cancelled — filter for Active only to eliminate stale contacts), original issue date, current expiration date, years licensed (2026 minus issue year), agency legal name (if affiliated with agency vs. individual DBA), agency address (street, city, state, ZIP), agency phone, agency email (from agency website), agent email (enrich via ZoomInfo/Apollo/LinkedIn for agency principals and independent agents), agent type (captive agent for single carrier like State Farm/Allstate/Nationwide exclusive agents vs. independent agent/broker representing multiple carriers, agency owner/principal with ownership stake vs. producer/agent employee, financial advisor holding insurance licenses for variable products), specialization/focus (infer from lines of authority: Personal Lines auto/home specialist, Commercial P&C for business insurance, Life Insurance specialist, Employee Benefits consultant for group health, Financial Services holding Life + Variable for annuities/investments), carrier appointments (some states disclose appointed carriers in public database showing which insurance companies the agent is authorized to sell for), disciplinary history flags (suspensions, revocations, consumer complaints, regulatory actions), and NIPR number for cross-state validation. Target all active full-time insurance producers: exclude inactive/expired/revoked licenses (no purchase intent), exclude CE provider licenses (these are for insurance instructors not agents), exclude adjuster-only licenses (claims adjusters don't sell insurance), exclude public adjuster licenses (different business model), filter for licenses with active status and recent renewal dates (past 2 years) to focus on currently practicing agents. Estimated 1.5M total licensed individuals per Insurance Agent Lists and NAIC data, filtering to 800K-1M active full-time agents (excluding part-time agents with primary careers outside insurance, inactive licenses maintained for CE consulting, lapsed licenses). Geographic concentration in high-population states: California 150K+ agents (largest market), Texas 125K+, Florida 110K+, New York 85K+, Pennsylvania 65K+, Illinois 60K+, Ohio 55K+, Georgia 50K+, North Carolina, Michigan, Arizona, Washington per state DOI annual reports. Data is 100% public: state insurance codes mandate public disclosure of producer licensing for consumer protection (verify agent credentials before purchasing insurance, check disciplinary history), with free online lookup portals and no authentication barriers — bulk downloads available in many states via open data initiatives or FOIA requests for full licensing databases in CSV format (California weekly updates, Florida quarterly snapshots). Email enrichment required since most state databases contain only agency mailing addresses: use ZoomInfo/Apollo for agency principals and independent brokers (business contact info), LinkedIn scraping for individual agents, agency website scraping for 'Contact Us' forms and agent bio pages listing direct emails/phones.
